summary: Isaiah 26 (21 verses) continues the story of holiness. Starting with 'In that day, this song will be sung in the land of Judah: “We have a strong city. God appoints salvation for walls and bulwarks.', it moves through themes of holiness, judgment and calls readers toward hope.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows holiness lived out in assyrian crisis, exile hope. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: In that day, this song will be sung in the land of Judah: “We have a strong city. God appoints salvation for walls and bulwarks.
Yahweh, your hand is lifted up, yet they don’t see; but they will see your zeal for the people and be disappointed. Yes, fire will consume your adversaries.
For, behold, Yahweh comes out of his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity. The earth also will disclose her blood, and will no longer cover her slain.

questions.question: What is happening in Isaiah 26?
questions.answer: In 21 verses, this chapter isaiah 26 (21 verses) continues the story of holiness. starting with 'in that day, this song will be sung in the land of judah: “we have a strong city. god appoints salvation for walls and bulwarks.', it moves through themes of holiness, judgment and calls readers toward hope. The setting is assyrian crisis, exile hope, written to judah. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Isaiah and why 26 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally isaiah son of amoz, addressed to judah around ~700 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophecy — its themes of holiness, judgment build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'righteousness' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Being in right standing, doing what is right. In this chapter, it appears in context of holiness. For a first-time reader: think of it as being in right standing, doing what is right, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through holiness and judgment, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 9 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'With my soul I have desired you in the night. Yes, with my spirit within me I will seek you earnestly; for when your judgments are on the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn ...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about holiness. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?

glossary.def: Being in right standing, doing what is right
